readings.c1s3:
¶
'''unrecoverably''' (un-rē-kuv′ėr-a-bli), ''adv.'' In an unrecoverable manner; irrecoverably; incurably.
{{smaller block|Long sick, and ''unrecoverably.''
{{right|''Bp. Hall,'' Meditations and Vows, ii.}}}}

'''unrecovered''' (un-rē-kuv′ėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not recovered; not found or restored.—'''2†.''' Irrecoverable. ''Chapman,'' Iliad, ix. 247. (''Davies.'')

'''unrecruitable''' (un-rẹ̄-krö′ta-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being recruited, in any sense. ''Milton,'' On Education.

'''unrecumbent''' (un-rē-kum′bent), ''a.'' Not reclining or reposing. ''Cowper,'' Morning Walk.

'''unrecuring†''' (un-rẹ̄-kūr′ing), ''a.'' Incapable of being cured; incurable. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Seeking to hide herself, as doth the deer
That hath received some ''unrecuring'' wound.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iii. 1. 90.}}}}

'''unredeemed''' (un-rẹ̄-dēmd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not redeemed; not ransomed: as, an ''unredeemed'' captive; an ''unredeemed'' sinner. ''Jer. Taylor,'' Sermons, III. ii.—'''2.''' Not recalled into the treasury or bank by payment of the value in money: as, ''unredeemed'' bills, notes, or stock.—'''3.''' Not fulfilled, as a promise or pledge.
{{smaller block|No one takes the trouble to recollect his contrary opinions or his ''unredeemed'' pledges.
{{right|''Macaulay,'' Athenian Orators.}}}}
'''4.''' Not counterbalanced or alleviated by any countervailing quality; unmitigated.

'''unreformedness''' (un-rē-fôr′med-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unreformed. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LIV. 345. [Rare.]

'''unregarded''' (un-rē-gär′ded), ''a.'' Not regarded; not heeded; not noticed; neglected; slighted.
{{smaller block|Since whose decease, learning lies ''unregarded.''
{{right|''Spenser'', Ruins of Time, l. 440.}}
The rifts where ''unregarded'' mosses be.
{{right|''Lowell'', Sea-Weed.}}}}

'''unregeneracy''' (un-rē-jen′e̤-rạ̄-si), ''n.'' The state of being unregenerate or unrenewed in heart. ''South'', Sermons.

'''unregenerate''' (un-rē-jen′e̤-rāt), ''a.'' Not regenerated; not renewed in heart; remaining at enmity with God; in a general sense, wicked; bad.
{{smaller block|''Unregenerate'' carnal man.
{{right|''Bp. Horsley'', Sermons, II. xx.}}}}

'''unregenerated''' (un-rē-jen′e̤-rā-ted), ''a.'' Same as ''unregenerate.''

'''unregeneration†''' (un-rē-jen-e̤-rā′sho̤n), ''n.'' The character or state of being unregenerate. ''Bp. Hall'', Repentance, viii. § 4.

'''unregistered''' (un-rej′is-tėrd), ''a.'' Not registered; not recorded.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hours
''Unregister’d'' in vulgar fame.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 13. 119.}}}}

'''unregretfulness''' (un-rē-gret′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unregretful; content.

'''unreigned†''', ''a.'' An obsolete spelling of ''unreined.''

'''unrein''' (un-rān′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''rein''<sup>1</sup>.] To loosen the rein of; give the rein to; allow to have free course.
readings.c3s1:

'''unrelentingly''' (un-rē-len′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an unrelenting manner; harshly; inexorably. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LII. 688.

'''unrelentingness''' (un-rē-len′ting-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unrelenting; severity; inexorableness.

'''unreliability''' (un-rē-lī-a̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' Unreliableness; untrustworthiness.

'''unreliable''' (un-rē-lī′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not reliable; not to be relied or depended on. ''Coleridge.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')
{{smaller block|Alcibiades, who might (chronologically speaking) have been the son of Pericles, was too unsteady, and (according to Mr. Coleridge’s coinage) ''unreliable;'' or, perhaps, in more correct English, too “unrelyuponable.”
{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, iii.}}}}

'''unreliableness''' (un-rē-lī′a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being unreliable. ''Coleridge.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')

'''unrelievable''' (un-rẹ̄-lē′va̤-bl), ''a.'' Admitting of no relief or succor.
{{smaller block|No degree of distress is ''unrelievable'' by his power.
{{right|''Boyle'', Works, I. 258.}}}}

'''unrelieved''' (un-rē-lēvd′), ''a.'' Not relieved, in any sense. ''Boyle.''

'''unrelievedly''' (un-rē-lē′ved-li), ''adv.'' Without relief or mitigation.
{{smaller block|The interest, intense as it is, is from first to last ''unrelievedly'' painful. {{right|''The Academy'', Nov. 30, 1889, p. 347.}}}}

'''unremediable''' (un-rē-mē′di-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Irremediable. ''Sir P. Sidney.''

'''unremembered''' (un-rē-mem′bėrd), ''a.'' Not remembered; forgotten.
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''unremittingly''' (un-rẹ̄-mit′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unremitting manner; without relaxing for a time; incessantly. ''Wordsworth'', Excursion, ix.

'''unremittingness''' (un-rẹ̄-mit′ing-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unremitting; continuousness.

'''unremorseful''' (un-rẹ̄-môrs′fu̇l), ''a.'' Feeling no remorse; unpitying; remorseless.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unremorseful'' fate
Did work the falls of those two princes dead.</poem>{{right|''Niccols'', Sir T. Overbury’s Vision, 1616. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unremorsefully''' (un-rẹ̄-môrs′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' Without remorse; unpityingly. ''Hawthorne'', Old Manse, p. 314.

'''unremorseless''' (un-rẹ̄-môrs′les), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> (here intensive) + ''remorseless.''] Showing or feeling no remorse; unpitying; remorseless. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>His mellifluous breath
Could not at all charm ''unremorseless'' death.</poem>{{right|''Cowley'', Elegy on Mr. Richard Clarke.}}}}

'''unremovable''' (un-rẹ̄-mö′va̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be removed; fixed; irremovable. ''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, i.

'''unremovableness''' (un-rẹ̄-mö′va̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being unremovable, irremovable, or immovable. ''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, iv.

'''unremovably''' (un-rẹ̄-mö′va̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unremovable manner; irremovably. ''Shak.'', T. of A., v. 2. 227.

¶
'''unremoved''' (un-rē-mövd′), ''a.'' Not removed; not taken away; hence, firm; unshaken.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unrecognizably|6640|unremoved}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|The opening through which we had come had closed ''unrecognizably'' behind us.
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LXVII. 499.}}}}

'''unrecognized''' (un-rek′o̤g-nīzd), ''a.'' Not recognized, in any sense.

{{smaller block|As dear Sam Johnson sits behind the screen, . . . there is no want of dignity in him, in that homely image of labour ill-rewarded, genius as yet ''unrecognised'', independence sturdy and uncomplaining.
{{right|''Thackeray'', On Screens in Dining-Rooms.}}}}

'''unrecommended''' (un-rek-o̤-men′ded), ''a.'' Not recommended; not favorably mentioned. ''V. Knox'', Essays, No. 113.

'''unrecompensed''' (un-rek′o̤m-penst), ''a.'' Not recompensed, rewarded, or requited.

{{smaller block|Heaven will not see so true a love ''unrecompens’d.''
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, iv. 3.}}}}

'''unreconcilable†''' (un-rek′o̤n-sī-la̤-bl), ''a.'' Irreconcilable. ''Bp. Hall'', No Peace with Rome.

'''unreconcilably†''' (un-rek′o̤n-sī-la̤-bli), ''adv.'' Irreconcilably. ''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, ii. 381.

'''unreconciled''' (un-rek′o̤n-sīld), ''a.'' Not reconciled. {{smaller|(''a'') Not made consistent: as, ''unreconciled'' statements. (''b'') Not restored to friendship or favor; still at enmity or opposition: as, a sinner ''unreconciled'' to God. (''c''†) Not atoned for.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Any crime
''Unreconciled'' as yet to heaven and grace.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 27.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d''†) Irreconcilable; implacable.}}
{{smaller block|I’m even he that once did owe ''unreconcil’d'' hate to you.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, iii. 2.}}}}

'''unreconciliable†''' (un-rek-o̤n-sil′i-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Unreconcilable. ''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 1. 47.

'''unreconstructed''' (un-rē-kon-struk′ted), ''a.'' Not reconstructed; specifically, in ''U. S. politics'', not yet reorganized as a State of the Union: applied to seceded States after the civil war; also, loosely, to citizens of the South not reconciled to the results of that war.
{{smaller block|On Thursday, Mr. Butler’s Committee on Reconstruction reported in favor of extending for a month the time during which an ''unreconstructed'' Southerner may retain his Government employment.
{{right|''The Nation'', VIII. 221.}}}}

'''unrecorded''' (un-rē-kôr′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not recorded; not registered; not made part of any record: as, an ''unrecorded'' deed or lease.
{{smaller block|The ''unrecorded'' English words actually in use among the people.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', X. 290.}}}}
'''2.''' Not kept in remembrance by writing or by public monuments.
{{smaller block|Not ''unrecorded'' in the rolls of fame.
{{right|''Pope.''}}}}

'''unrecounted''' (un-rẹ̄-koun′ted), ''a.'' Not recounted; not related or recited. ''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iii. 2. 48.

'''unrecoverable''' (un-rē-kuv′ėr-a-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Incapable of being recovered, found, restored, or obtained again; not obtainable from a debtor; irrecoverable: as, an ''unrecoverable'' article of property; an ''unrecoverable'' debt.
{{smaller block|I have a great many debts due to me in America, and I had rather they should remain ''unrecoverable'' by any law than submit to the Stamp Act.
{{right|''Franklin'', Autobiog., p. 369.}}}}
'''2.''' Not capable of recovering; incurable; irremediable.
{{smaller block|’Tis the dead palsy, that, without almost a miracle, leaves a man ''unrecoverable.''
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, ii. 14.}}
Loss of memory is so commonly associated with ''unrecoverable'' cases.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Psychol.'', I. 333.}}}}

'''unrecoverably''' (un-rē-kuv′ėr-a-bli), ''adv.'' In an unrecoverable manner; irrecoverably; incurably.
{{smaller block|Long sick, and ''unrecoverably.''
{{right|''Bp. Hall,'' Meditations and Vows, ii.}}}}

'''unrecovered''' (un-rē-kuv′ėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not recovered; not found or restored.—'''2†.''' Irrecoverable. ''Chapman,'' Iliad, ix. 247. (''Davies.'')

'''unrecruitable''' (un-rẹ̄-krö′ta-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being recruited, in any sense. ''Milton,'' On Education.

'''unrecumbent''' (un-rē-kum′bent), ''a.'' Not reclining or reposing. ''Cowper,'' Morning Walk.

'''unrecuring†''' (un-rẹ̄-kūr′ing), ''a.'' Incapable of being cured; incurable. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Seeking to hide herself, as doth the deer
That hath received some ''unrecuring'' wound.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iii. 1. 90.}}}}

'''unredeemed''' (un-rẹ̄-dēmd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not redeemed; not ransomed: as, an ''unredeemed'' captive; an ''unredeemed'' sinner. ''Jer. Taylor,'' Sermons, III. ii.—'''2.''' Not recalled into the treasury or bank by payment of the value in money: as, ''unredeemed'' bills, notes, or stock.—'''3.''' Not fulfilled, as a promise or pledge.
{{smaller block|No one takes the trouble to recollect his contrary opinions or his ''unredeemed'' pledges.
{{right|''Macaulay,'' Athenian Orators.}}}}
'''4.''' Not counterbalanced or alleviated by any countervailing quality; unmitigated. {{smaller block|The ''unredeemed'' ugliness . . . of a slothful people.
{{right|''Carlyle.''}}}}
'''5.''' Not taken out of pledge or pawn.
{{smaller block|Pawnbrokers lose on an average 10 per cent. on ''unredeemed'' goods. ''The Echo'', Jan. 14, 1888. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}

'''unreduct†''' (un-rẹ̄-dukt′), ''a.'' Not reduced.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thought ''unreduct'' to act
Is but an embryon in the truest sense.</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', Family of Love, iii. 1.}}}}

'''unreel''' (un-rēl′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''reel''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To unwind from a reel, as a line or thread.
{{smaller block|A measured mile course was laid off, ''unreeling'' from an anchored stake buoy one mile of fine wire.
{{right|''The Engineer'', LXVIII. 413.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become unwound from a reel.
{{smaller block|The line will ''unreel'' faster than it is needed, and get into a snarl. ''Tribune Book of Sports'', p. 163.}}

'''unreeve''' (un-rēv′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unreeved'', ''unrove'', ppr. ''unreeving''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''reeve''<sup>3</sup>.] ''Naut.'', to withdraw or take out (a rope) from a block, thimble, etc.

'''unrefined''' (un-rẹ̄-fīnd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not refined; not purified: as, ''unrefined'' sugar.—'''2.''' Not refined or polished in manners, taste, or the like.
{{smaller block|These early and ''unrefined'' ages.
{{right|''Burke'', Vind. of Nat. Society.}}}}

'''unreformable''' (un-rẹ̄-fôr′ma̤-bl), ''a.'' Not reformable; not capable of being reformed or amended. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, vii. § 24.

'''unreformation''' (un-ref-ọr-mā′shon), ''n.'' The state of being unreformed; want of reformation. ''Bp. Hall'', Sermons, Eccles. iii. 4. [Rare.]

'''unreformedness''' (un-rē-fôr′med-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unreformed. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LIV. 345. [Rare.]

'''unregarded''' (un-rē-gär′ded), ''a.'' Not regarded; not heeded; not noticed; neglected; slighted.
{{smaller block|Since whose decease, learning lies ''unregarded.''
{{right|''Spenser'', Ruins of Time, l. 440.}}
The rifts where ''unregarded'' mosses be.
{{right|''Lowell'', Sea-Weed.}}}}

'''unregeneracy''' (un-rē-jen′e̤-rạ̄-si), ''n.'' The state of being unregenerate or unrenewed in heart. ''South'', Sermons.

'''unregenerate''' (un-rē-jen′e̤-rāt), ''a.'' Not regenerated; not renewed in heart; remaining at enmity with God; in a general sense, wicked; bad.
{{smaller block|''Unregenerate'' carnal man.
{{right|''Bp. Horsley'', Sermons, II. xx.}}}}

'''unregenerated''' (un-rē-jen′e̤-rā-ted), ''a.'' Same as ''unregenerate.''

'''unregeneration†''' (un-rē-jen-e̤-rā′sho̤n), ''n.'' The character or state of being unregenerate. ''Bp. Hall'', Repentance, viii. § 4.

'''unregistered''' (un-rej′is-tėrd), ''a.'' Not registered; not recorded.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hours
''Unregister’d'' in vulgar fame.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 13. 119.}}}}

'''unregretfulness''' (un-rē-gret′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unregretful; content.

'''unreigned†''', ''a.'' An obsolete spelling of ''unreined.''

'''unrein''' (un-rān′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''rein''<sup>1</sup>.] To loosen the rein of; give the rein to; allow to have free course.
<poem>How negligently graceful he ''unreins''
His verse, and writes in loose familiar strains!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Addison'', The Greatest English Poets.}}}}

'''unreined''' (un-rānd′), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''unreigned''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''reined'', pp. of ''rein''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' Not restrained by the reins or bridle. ''Milton'', P. L., vii. 17.—'''2.''' Not held in proper sway or subjection; unchecked.

{{smaller block|This wild ''unreigned'' multitude. ''Daniel'', Civil Wars, vi.}}

'''unrejoicing''' (un-rē-joi′sing), ''a.'' Unjoyous; gloomy; sad.

{{smaller block|Here winter holds his ''unrejoicing'' court.
{{right|''Thomson'', Winter.}}}}

'''unrelated''' (un-rē-lā′ted), ''a.'' Not related, in any sense. ''Barrow'', Sermons, III. 3.

'''unrelative''' (un-rel′a̤-tiv), ''a.'' Not relative, in any sense.

{{smaller block|If you pitch upon the treaty of Munster, do not interrupt it by dipping and deviating into other books ''unrelative'' to it. {{right|''Clarendon.''}}}}

'''unrelaxed''' (un-rē-lakst′), ''a.'' Not relaxed; strained; determined.

{{smaller block|And even in his best passages, the strained expression, the ''unrelaxed'' determination to be vigorous, grows wearisome. {{right|''The Academy'', April 4, 1891, p. 320.}}}}

'''unrelenting''' (un-rē-len′ting), ''a.'' That does not or will not relent; not being or becoming lenient, mild, gentle, or merciful; continuing to be hard, severe, pitiless, hostile, or cold; inexorable; unyielding.

<poem>The ireful arm
Of ''unrelenting'' Clifford.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 1. 58.}} ciless, hard-hearted, unsparing, unpitying, rigorous, cruel.}}

'''unrelentingly''' (un-rē-len′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an unrelenting manner; harshly; inexorably. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LII. 688.

'''unrelentingness''' (un-rē-len′ting-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unrelenting; severity; inexorableness.

'''unreliability''' (un-rē-lī-a̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' Unreliableness; untrustworthiness.

'''unreliable''' (un-rē-lī′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not reliable; not to be relied or depended on. ''Coleridge.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')
{{smaller block|Alcibiades, who might (chronologically speaking) have been the son of Pericles, was too unsteady, and (according to Mr. Coleridge’s coinage) ''unreliable;'' or, perhaps, in more correct English, too “unrelyuponable.”
{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, iii.}}}}

'''unreliableness''' (un-rē-lī′a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being unreliable. ''Coleridge.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')

'''unrelievable''' (un-rẹ̄-lē′va̤-bl), ''a.'' Admitting of no relief or succor.
{{smaller block|No degree of distress is ''unrelievable'' by his power.
{{right|''Boyle'', Works, I. 258.}}}}

'''unrelieved''' (un-rē-lēvd′), ''a.'' Not relieved, in any sense. ''Boyle.''

'''unrelievedly''' (un-rē-lē′ved-li), ''adv.'' Without relief or mitigation.
{{smaller block|The interest, intense as it is, is from first to last ''unrelievedly'' painful. {{right|''The Academy'', Nov. 30, 1889, p. 347.}}}}

'''unremediable''' (un-rē-mē′di-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Irremediable. ''Sir P. Sidney.''

'''unremembered''' (un-rē-mem′bėrd), ''a.'' Not remembered; forgotten. {{smaller block|Nor must their [Nobles and People of Scotland] sincere and moderate proceedings hitherto be ''unremember’d.''
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}}

'''unremembering''' (un-rē-mem′bėr-ing), ''a.'' Having no memory or recollection.

{{smaller block|''Unrememb’ring'' of its former pain. ''Dryden'', Æneid, vi.}}

'''unremembrance''' (un-rẹ̄-mem′brans), ''n.'' Forgetfulness; want of remembrance. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Some words are negative in their original language, but seem positive, because their negation is unknown: as, amnesty, an ''unremembrance'', or general pardon.
{{right|''Watts'', Logic, i. 4.}}}}

'''unremitted''' (un-rẹ̄-mit′ed), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not remitted; not forgiven: as, punishment ''unremitted.''—'''2.''' Not having a temporary relaxation: as, pain ''unremitted.''

{{smaller block|It is the strongest motive that we can suggest for ''unremitted'' diligence in the acquisition of useful knowledge.
{{right|''Everett'', Orations, I. 268.}}}}

'''unremittedly''' (un-rẹ̄-mit′ed-li), ''adv.'' In an unremitted manner; incessantly; continuously.

{{smaller block|Newport has an advantage which Swansea has been striving for ''unremittedly.'' ''The Engineer'', LXVII. 408.}}

'''unremitting''' (un-rẹ̄-mit′ing), ''a.'' Not abating; not relaxing for a time; incessant; continued: as, ''unremitting'' exertions.

<poem>How many a rustic Milton has passed by,
Stifling the speechless longings of his heart
In ''unremitting'' drudgery and care!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shelley'', Queen Mab, v.}}}}

'''unremittingly''' (un-rẹ̄-mit′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unremitting manner; without relaxing for a time; incessantly. ''Wordsworth'', Excursion, ix.

'''unremittingness''' (un-rẹ̄-mit′ing-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unremitting; continuousness.

'''unremorseful''' (un-rẹ̄-môrs′fu̇l), ''a.'' Feeling no remorse; unpitying; remorseless.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unremorseful'' fate
Did work the falls of those two princes dead.</poem>{{right|''Niccols'', Sir T. Overbury’s Vision, 1616. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unremorsefully''' (un-rẹ̄-môrs′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' Without remorse; unpityingly. ''Hawthorne'', Old Manse, p. 314.

'''unremorseless''' (un-rẹ̄-môrs′les), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> (here intensive) + ''remorseless.''] Showing or feeling no remorse; unpitying; remorseless. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>His mellifluous breath
Could not at all charm ''unremorseless'' death.</poem>{{right|''Cowley'', Elegy on Mr. Richard Clarke.}}}}

'''unremovable''' (un-rẹ̄-mö′va̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be removed; fixed; irremovable. ''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, i.

'''unremovableness''' (un-rẹ̄-mö′va̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being unremovable, irremovable, or immovable. ''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, iv.

'''unremovably''' (un-rẹ̄-mö′va̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unremovable manner; irremovably. ''Shak.'', T. of A., v. 2. 227.

'''unremoved''' (un-rē-mövd′), ''a.'' Not removed; not taken away; hence, firm; unshaken.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
